notions.question: How do British institutions work without a single written constitution?
notions.definition: The United Kingdom is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary system. Its constitution is not codified in a single text: it rests on Acts of Parliament (statutes), court decisions, constitutional conventions and historical documents. The Westminster Parliament comprises the monarch, the House of Commons, elected by universal suffrage (650 seats), and the House of Lords, which is unelected (appointed life peers, a limited number of hereditary peers, bishops of the Church of England). Under the principle of parliamentary sovereignty, Parliament can pass or repeal any law. The Prime Minister is the leader of the party that holds a majority in the Commons; he or she forms the government and the Cabinet, which are collectively responsible to the Commons. The monarch reigns but does not rule.

lignes: Head of State; symbolic and ceremonial role (Royal Assent to bills, King's/Queen's Speech)
650 elected Members of Parliament (MPs); passes laws and the budget; scrutinises the government
Unelected chamber; examines and amends bills; power of delay limited by the Parliament Acts (1911, 1949)
Government drawn from the majority in the Commons, collective responsibility
Second-largest party in the Commons, "shadow cabinet"

termes.definition: A monarchy whose powers are limited by the constitution.
The supremacy of Acts of Parliament.
The Opposition team that mirrors the ministers.

exemple.texte: In a commentary, one would point out that a British Prime Minister can change in the middle of a Parliament without a general election, when his or her party changes leader: it is the majority in the Commons, not a direct popular vote, that underpins the Prime Minister's power.

confusions.explication: The United Kingdom does have a constitution, but it is spread across statutes, conventions and case law.

notions.question: Why do two parties dominate British political life?
notions.definition: General elections to the House of Commons use the single-member plurality system (first past the post): in each of the 650 constituencies, the candidate who comes first is elected, even without an absolute majority. This system favours the two main parties, the Conservative Party ("Tories") and the Labour Party, and disadvantages parties whose votes are spread thinly (Liberal Democrats, Reform UK, Greens), while allowing regionally concentrated parties (Scottish National Party) to win many seats. It often produces clear majorities on a minority of the vote. A 2011 referendum rejected a switch to the Alternative Vote. The July 2024 general election returned Labour to power with a large majority.

lignes: Moderate left; public services, historically the trade unions

termes.es: sistema mayoritario uninominal a una vuelta
termes.definition: The candidate who comes first is elected.
An area that elects one MP.

exemple.texte: With 35% of the vote spread evenly, one party can win more than half the seats; with 15% spread thinly, another may win only a handful: this is the amplifying effect of the plurality system.

confusions.explication: Historical terms; "Tory" is still commonly used to mean a Conservative.

The House of Lords is elected by universal suffrage
The Prime Minister is the leader of the majority party in the Commons

choix.explication: The monarch reigns but does not rule.

questions.enonce: Which electoral system is used to elect the House of Commons?

choix.explication: The candidate who comes first wins.

flashcards.question: Outline British institutions and the electoral system.
flashcards.reponse: Constitutional monarchy, parliamentary system, uncodified constitution (statutes, conventions, case law), parliamentary sovereignty. Parliament: monarch, House of Commons (650 elected MPs), House of Lords (unelected, limited power of delay). Prime Minister = leader of the majority party in the Commons; Cabinet collectively responsible; Opposition and shadow cabinet. First past the post → two-party system Conservatives / Labour, clear majorities, thinly spread parties disadvantaged, SNP favoured by its concentration.
erreurs: Saying that the United Kingdom has no constitution
